extraction_text: Yudhishthira requests Bhishma to explain the principles of Samkhya philosophy.
Bhishma agrees to explain the pure principles of Samkhya established by sages like Kapila.

Bhishma explains the knowledge of all objects having defects, including various beings like humans, Pisacas, Rakshasas, Yakshas, Nagas, Gandharvas, ancestors, animals, Garuda, Maruts, royal sages, Brahmin sages, Asuras, Vishvadevas, Devas, Yogins, Prajapatis, and Brahma.
Bhishma describes understanding the highest lifespan, supreme nature of happiness, and consequences of pursuing sensory objects.
Bhishma explains understanding the merits and demerits of heaven, Vedic doctrines, Yoga, and Samkhya.
Bhishma details the qualities of the three gunas: Sattva (10 qualities), Rajas (9 qualities), Tamas (8 qualities), and the evolution of consciousness.
Bhishma describes the path of purification through knowledge and good deeds leading to liberation.
Bhishma explains the attachments of senses to their objects and the cosmic chain of dependencies.

attributes.structure: Chain of dependencies from senses to ultimate reality

extraction_text: Bhishma describes the dependencies: eyes to form, nose to smell, ears to sound, tongue to taste, body to touch, wind to space, ignorance to Tamas, desire to sensory objects, Vishnu to strides, Indra to strength, fire to stomach, earth to water, water to fire, fire to wind, wind to space, space to Mahat, Mahat to consciousness, consciousness to Tamas, Tamas to Rajas, Rajas to Sattva, Sattva to soul, soul to Narayana, Narayana to liberation, and liberation to nothing.
Bhishma explains understanding the body containing Sattva with 16 qualities, with Prakriti and mind attached to body while soul remains neutral.
Bhishma describes understanding the senses and their objects attached to soul, and the five vital winds.

elements: Vital winds (Prana, Apana, Samana, Udana, Vyana)

extraction_text: Bhishma mentions seven winds and seven qualities, along with understanding Prajapatis, great paths, seven sages, and royal sages.
Bhishma concludes by noting that even great sages and deities eventually fall from their high positions after long periods.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about the defects of the human body.
Bhishma explains the five defects of the human body according to Kapila's Sankhya philosophy.
Bhishma describes how to overcome these defects through specific virtues.
Bhishma discusses the understanding of merits, defects, and causes through hundreds of examples.
Bhishma describes the illusory nature of the world.

attributes.description: The world is like water bubbles, full of Vishnu's illusions, like a painting, like hollow reeds

extraction_text: The wise Sankhya philosophers, relying on profound Sankhya knowledge, abandon the body that produces offspring.

They use the sword of knowledge and the staff of asceticism to swiftly eliminate the foul odors of Rajas (passion), the stench of Tamas (ignorance), and the fragrance of Sattva (goodness) produced by bodily contact.

They use wisdom to cross the terrible ocean of life, which is full of the water of suffering, with anxiety and sorrow as its great lakes, disease and death as its crocodiles, and great terror as its snakes.
Successful sages cross this difficult-to-cross ocean of life through yoga and enter the pure sky.
The sun's rays carry these Sankhya philosophers of pure conduct, just as fibers in a lotus stem carry nutrients.
The wind carries successful Yatis (ascetics) who are courageous, have abandoned desire, and have asceticism as their wealth.
The wind, which is the best of the seven Maruts (wind gods), blows in the auspicious world - subtle, cool, fragrant, and comfortable - and carries them to the supreme abode of space.
Space carries them to the supreme abode of Rajas, Rajas carries them to the supreme abode of Sattva, and Sattva carries them to the great god Narayana.
The pure-souled great god personally carries them to the Supreme Soul, where these pure people reach the Supreme Soul, become one with it, attain immortality, and do not return.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma whether those who reach the supreme state remember their previous births and deaths, and expresses concern that if liberated beings retain consciousness, it would be a great flaw in liberation.
The speaker addresses the listener as 'child' and acknowledges the difficulty of the question, stating even wise people are confused by it.
The speaker explains the nature of the soul (atman) according to the Sankhya philosophy, describing how the subtle soul uses the senses as instruments.

supernatural_elements: Description of the soul's nature and its relationship with senses

extraction_text: The speaker describes how the soul remains awake while the senses sleep, and how it wanders freely like the wind.

supernatural_elements: Soul's ability to wander independently of the body

extraction_text: The speaker explains that the soul pervades all qualities (sattva, rajas, tamas), all elements (earth, water, fire, air, ether), and all aspects of consciousness.

supernatural_elements: Soul's omnipresence in all aspects of existence

extraction_text: The speaker describes how the soul transcends primordial matter (prakriti) and merges with the supreme soul (paramatman), which is identified with Narayana.

supernatural_elements: Soul's transcendence and merger with the divine

extraction_text: The speaker explains that those who pursue liberation through this knowledge soon attain peace, and Sankhya practitioners reach the highest destination through this knowledge.

relationships: Path to liberation for spiritual seekers

extraction_text: The speaker praises Sankhya knowledge as supreme, ancient, eternal, indestructible, and identical with Brahman, and states it is praised by Brahmins, gods, and learned people.

relationships: Recognition by divine and learned beings

extraction_text: The speaker concludes by stating that Sankhya knowledge is found in the Vedas, Puranas, historical legends, and even worldly knowledge, and that among living beings, the mobile ones (animals) are superior to immobile ones.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about the imperishable and perishable, seeking knowledge before Bhishma's impending death.

relationships: Yudhishthira is Bhishma's grandnephew and student
Bhishma is the Kuru elder and teacher

extraction_text: Bhishma responds by recounting an ancient dialogue between Sage Vasistha and King Janaka.
King Janaka approaches Sage Vasistha, seeking knowledge of the supreme, eternal Brahman.

relationships: King Janaka is a disciple seeking enlightenment from Sage Vasistha

extraction_text: Sage Vasistha begins to explain the nature of cosmic cycles, the perishable world, and the imperishable Brahman.

supernatural_elements: Description of cosmic time (yugas, kalpas, Brahma's day/night)
The imperishable Brahman as eternal and unchanging

extraction_text: The text describes the cosmic creation process and the nature of existence according to philosophical teachings.

characters: The Supreme Being (referred to as Prajapati, Vishnu, or the Unmanifest)

extraction_text: The Supreme Being (Prajapati) is described as all-pervading, with hands, feet, heads, mouths, eyes, and ears everywhere.
The golden womb (Hiranyagarbha) is identified as consciousness (Buddhi), also called Mahat or Virinchi in different traditions.

attributes.action: Identification with consciousness and various names

extraction_text: It has many forms and is the universal soul, the only imperishable entity, encompassing the entire triple world with its diversity.
Through transformation, it creates itself, giving rise to self-awareness (Ahamkara) and the self-aware creator (Prajapati).

attributes.relationships: The Supreme Being creates Ahamkara and Prajapati

extraction_text: The manifest arises from the unmanifest, termed the creation of knowledge, while Mahat (consciousness) and self-awareness are creations of ignorance.

attributes.action: Distinction between creations of knowledge and ignorance

extraction_text: From self-awareness, a third creation emerges, and from that, a fourth creation arises through transformation.
The five elements (wind, fire, space, water, earth) and the five subtle elements (sound, touch, form, taste, smell) appear simultaneously as the fifth creation.
The five sense organs (ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose) and five action organs (speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals) arise along with the mind.

attributes.action: Formation of perceptual and active faculties

extraction_text: These constitute the twenty-four principles (Tattvas) present in all forms, understood by wise Brahmins who thus avoid sorrow.
All beings across the three worlds—gods, humans, demons, and various creatures—possess bodies composed of these elements and are subject to destruction.

characters: All Beings (Gods, Humans, Demons, Animals, etc.)

extraction_text: The imperishable is described: the world perishes, filled with ignorance, as the unmanifest becomes manifest.

attributes.action: Contrast between perishable world and imperishable reality

extraction_text: Vishnu is identified as the twenty-fifth Tattva, transcending yet supporting the other twenty-four, considered the basis by the wise.
The unmanifest creates the manifest; the twenty-four Tattvas are manifest, while the twenty-fifth is unmanifest.

attributes.action: Distinction between manifest and unmanifest principles

extraction_text: Vishnu resides in the hearts of all forms, endowing the formless mind with all forms and eternal contemplation, acquiring creative and destructive qualities.
The text describes the process of the soul (purusha) becoming entangled with material nature (prakriti) through ignorance.

attributes.relationships: The Purusha, originally without qualities, becomes associated with and identifies itself with the qualities (gunas) of Prakriti due to ignorance (avidya).

extraction_text: The soul, due to ignorance, serves the foolish, enters various wombs, and becomes bound to the three qualities (gunas): Tamas (darkness/inertia), Rajas (passion/activity), and Sattva (goodness/purity).

attributes.relationships: The soul becomes bound to the cycle of rebirth (samsara) and identifies with its temporary abodes.

extraction_text: The text explains the three colors of Prakriti: white (Sattva), red (Rajas), and black (Tamas).
It describes the consequences of attachment to each guna: attachment to Tamas leads to hell, to Rajas leads to human rebirth, and to Sattva leads to heaven.

attributes.relationships: The soul's future state is determined by its predominant attachment to one of the three gunas.

extraction_text: Further elaboration: performing only evil deeds leads to rebirth as an animal; mixed deeds lead to human rebirth; consistently good deeds lead to rebirth as a deity.
The wise conclude that the perishable belongs to the realm of the Unmanifest (Prakriti), while the 25th principle (Purusha) operates through knowledge.

attributes.relationships: A fundamental distinction is made between the perishable material realm (Prakriti) and the eternal conscious principle (Purusha), with liberation coming through knowledge (jnana) of this distinction.

extraction_text: The text is identified as Chapter 291 of the Shanti Parva (Book of Peace) from the Mahabharata.
